title: PII Redaction
description: Redact a medical note with word-boundary regexes — string scan that replaces any SSN pattern and each sensitive term case-insensitively, counting replacements via a replacer callback.

conversation.intro: How a conversation about PII redaction would actually play out — a paralegal needs to send a medical narrative to opposing counsel and wants names + SSNs scrubbed before it goes out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down what counts as PII and what 'redact' means.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm given a body of free text plus a list of sensitive terms (names of people, places, etc.). I need to produce the same text with two kinds of patterns replaced by `[REDACTED]`: (1) US SSN patterns like `###-##-####`, and (2) any whole-word occurrence of a sensitive term, case-insensitive. Output is the redacted text plus a count of how many redactions fired."

Clarifiers first:
• What PII patterns are in scope? SSN definitely; what about emails, phone numbers, MRNs (medical record numbers), DOBs, addresses? Each has its own regex and its own false-positive profile.
• Strict SSN format `###-##-####` only, or also `#########` (no dashes) and `### ## ####` (spaces)? More permissive = more catches AND more false positives.
• Whole word matching for terms — what's a word? `\b` in JS uses ASCII word chars, so 'O'Brien' would split at the apostrophe; for European names that's wrong. Worth flagging.
• Case-insensitive on terms — `Jane`, `JANE`, `jane`, `JaNe` all redact. Good default.
• If a term contains regex metacharacters (a doctor's name like 'Dr.' or a hyphenated 'Anne-Marie') — treat as literal? Yes; escape before building the regex.
• Overlapping patterns — what if a term is itself a substring of an SSN? `\b...\b` prevents that, but worth confirming the spec.
• What's the output on no-redactions — same text, count 0? Or some signal that the doc was checked? Probably just the same text + 0.
• Logging the redactions — needed for chain-of-custody? Out of scope for the function, but the count is a foothold for that audit trail.
sections.why: The 'what's a word' clarifier is the load-bearing one — `\b` in JS regex is ASCII-only, so 'café' would have a word boundary between 'caf' and 'é' depending on the engine. For European names that's a real bug. The 'escape regex metacharacters' question is the one that distinguishes 'works on Jane and Smith' from 'works on Dr. Smith' — if you don't escape the `.`, the regex matches any char in that position and produces wrong redactions. Naming the false-positive profile (permissive SSN catches more but also bites '555-12-3456' inside an unrelated case-number) shows you've thought about the tradeoff.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: What's the obvious-but-fragile way to do this?
sections.say:
"The brute force is `text.split(' ').map(token => sensitiveSet.has(token) ? '[REDACTED]' : token).join(' ')`. Looks O(n) and simple — but it's broken in three ways. (1) Punctuation: 'Jane,' is one token, doesn't match 'Jane'. (2) Case: 'JANE' is a different string from 'Jane'. (3) Word-internal matches: it can't redact 'Jane' inside '...Jane reported pain.' because the tokenization is wrong relative to what's actually a word boundary in English.

The right approach is regex with word boundaries: `\b...\b` anchors the match to whole words regardless of surrounding punctuation. `g` flag for all occurrences. `i` flag for case-insensitive. And a replacer CALLBACK so we can both substitute AND count — `text.replace(re, () => { count++; return '[REDACTED]'; })`. That gives us the count for audit purposes 'for free' as part of the same scan.

For the SSN, the regex is `/\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b/g` — literal pattern, no user input, so no escaping needed. For each sensitive TERM, we have to escape regex metacharacters first because the term comes from user input."
sections.why: Naming all three failure modes of the split-and-check brute force is what proves you've actually thought about why regex is necessary — interview candidates who jump straight to regex often can't articulate what regex gives them that simpler code doesn't. The replacer-callback insight is the senior touch: it threads a side-effect counter through what is otherwise a pure-function call, which is exactly the technique you'd use for logging hits in a production redactor.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — regex scan with escape + counted replacer
sections.prompt: What are the load-bearing pieces and why?
sections.say:
"This is a multi-pattern regex scan over a single string. Two patterns: one hardcoded (SSN), one parameterized (each user term). Both use the same template:
• `\b...\b` word boundaries — anchor to whole tokens. 'Smith' doesn't match inside 'Smithson'. 'Jan' doesn't match inside 'January'.
• `g` flag — replace every occurrence, not just the first. Without it, 'Jane saw Jane' only redacts the first Jane.
• `i` flag — case-insensitive. Catches 'JANE', 'jane', 'Jane'.
• Replacer callback `() => { count++; return '[REDACTED]'; }` — increments the counter on every hit AND returns the replacement string. The callback fires per match, so the count is exact.

The ONE extra step for user terms: escape regex metacharacters before building the RegExp. `term.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` — for each metacharacter in the term, prepend a backslash. So 'Dr.' becomes 'Dr\\.' which the RegExp constructor sees as literal 'Dr.'. The `$&` in the replacement string is 'the matched character'. Without this step, a term like 'a+b' would parse as 'one-or-more a followed by b' rather than the literal string 'a+b'.

Processing order: SSN first, then each term in input order. Doesn't actually matter for correctness here (they're all on disjoint word boundaries normally), but it's stable — the same input produces the same redacted output every time."
sections.why: Spelling out what each regex feature buys you (`\b` → whole-word, `g` → all-occurrences, `i` → case-insensitive) is what proves you didn't just memorize the flags. The replacer-callback explanation is the senior move: most candidates use the string-substitution form `text.replace(re, '[REDACTED]')` and lose the count. The escape step is the security/correctness call-out — passing user input directly into a RegExp constructor without escaping is a regex-injection bug, and naming it shows you'd defend against malformed inputs.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a couple of inputs to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me trace." Three cases — the L3 note with two distinct names and one SSN, a clean no-PII text where count must be 0, and a multi-SSN-only case to prove the SSN regex catches multiple hits.

examples.input: 'Patient Jane Doe, SSN 123-45-6789, treated by Dr. Smith. Jane reported pain.', terms=['Jane','Smith']
examples.output: 'Patient [REDACTED] Doe, SSN [REDACTED], treated by Dr. [REDACTED]. [REDACTED] reported pain.' count=4
examples.note: The L3 input. One SSN (1 hit), 'Jane' appears twice (2 hits), 'Smith' once (1 hit) → count = 4. Note 'Smith' redacts inside 'Dr. Smith' because the period and space are word boundaries; if the text said 'Smithson' it would NOT redact, thanks to `\b` after 'Smith'.
examples.trace:
out = original text, count = 0
Step 1 — SSN sweep: /\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b/g finds '123-45-6789' (1 hit) → replace with [REDACTED], count=1
  out: 'Patient Jane Doe, SSN [REDACTED], treated by Dr. Smith. Jane reported pain.'
Step 2 — term 'Jane': escape (no metachars) → /\bJane\b/gi finds 2 hits → count=3
  out: 'Patient [REDACTED] Doe, SSN [REDACTED], treated by Dr. Smith. [REDACTED] reported pain.'
Step 3 — term 'Smith': escape (no metachars) → /\bSmith\b/gi finds 1 hit → count=4
  out: 'Patient [REDACTED] Doe, SSN [REDACTED], treated by Dr. [REDACTED]. [REDACTED] reported pain.'
return { text: out, count: 4 } ✓

examples.note: No-PII case — proves that 0-hit sweeps are no-ops. SSN regex matches nothing, 'Foo' regex matches nothing, count stays 0, text unchanged.
examples.trace:
out = 'Plain text no PII.', count = 0
SSN sweep: 0 hits, count=0, out unchanged
term 'Foo' sweep: 0 hits, count=0, out unchanged
return { text: 'Plain text no PII.', count: 0 } ✓

examples.note: Multi-SSN, empty-terms case. The `g` flag is what catches both SSNs in one scan. Empty terms list means the for-loop body never runs — count stays at whatever the SSN sweep produced.
examples.trace:
out = original text, count = 0
SSN sweep: /\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b/g finds 2 hits (111-22-3333, 444-55-6666). Each fires the callback: count++ then return [REDACTED]. After scan, count=2.
  out: 'Two SSNs: [REDACTED] and [REDACTED].'
term loop: terms=[] — body doesn't execute
return { text: out, count: 2 } ✓

sections.why: The L3 trace is the proof that the count arithmetic works — 1 SSN + 2 Janes + 1 Smith = 4, and the replacer fires once per match by design. The no-PII case is the boring sanity check that 0-hit sweeps don't break anything (some careless implementations return undefined or NaN for count). The multi-SSN case isolates the `g` flag — without it, only the first SSN would redact and count would be 1, which is the most common 'this looks like a bug to me' regex mistake.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases / failure modes / partial PII
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges and failure modes worth flagging:
• Partial PII — '12-345-6789' (off by one in the format) → SSN regex doesn't match. False NEGATIVE. If the spec is 'catch anything that looks like an SSN, even malformed', we'd loosen the regex (e.g. `\d{3}[- ]?\d{2}[- ]?\d{4}`) and accept more false positives.
• Phone number that looks like an SSN — '800-12-3456' is a real-format phone number, matches the SSN regex. False positive. The same regex over-matches anything that fits the digit-count-and-dash shape. For high-precision redaction, you'd validate the area-of-document context first.
• Term that's a substring of another word — 'Cat' in 'catastrophe'. `\b` prevents this: 'cat' inside 'catastrophe' has 'c' (word char) on both sides at the boundary, no `\b` match.
• Term that's at string boundaries — 'Jane' at the very start of the text. `\b` matches the start-of-string as a word boundary too, so the leading 'Jane' redacts.
• Term with regex metacharacters — 'Dr.', 'a+b', 'O'Brien' (apostrophe). The escape step `term.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` neutralizes the metacharacters. Without escape, 'Dr.' would match 'Drx', 'Dry', etc.
• Unicode names — 'José', 'O'Brien'. `\b` is ASCII-only in JS regex (unless you use the `u` flag with `\p{L}` classes). For multilingual support you'd switch to `/\p{L}+/gu` style boundaries.
• Empty terms list → for-loop is a no-op, only SSN sweep runs. Returns the SSN-redacted text + the SSN count. Cheap and works.
• Empty input text → both sweeps replace nothing, returns `{ text: '', count: 0 }`.
• Term that already IS '[REDACTED]' → if a user passes 'REDACTED' as a sensitive term, the second pass over already-redacted text would re-process them. Not a correctness bug (idempotent), but the count would inflate. Defensively, you could skip the brackets in the redaction tag.
• Order-dependence within terms — if term A's match overlaps with term B's, the order of the for-loop matters. With `\b` boundaries this is rare, but worth mentioning.
• Performance on huge text + huge term list — each term builds a new RegExp and scans the whole text. That's O(text * terms). For a 1MB text with 1000 terms, you'd want to combine all terms into one alternation regex `/(term1|term2|...)/gi`, scanning once."
sections.why: The 'phone that looks like SSN' false-positive is the kind of domain insight that distinguishes pattern matching from real PII detection — a junior candidate says 'we use a regex' and a senior says 'and here's the false-positive profile we accept'. The Unicode call-out and the alternation-regex optimization are both unprompted senior touches that show scope thinking. The 'already-redacted text re-processing' point is the kind of subtle idempotency question that interviewers love when they want to push beyond the happy path.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O((1 + k) * L) where L is the text length and k is the number of sensitive terms. One SSN sweep over the text (O(L)), then k term sweeps each O(L) — for k terms total. Each sweep is linear because regex matching with a non-pathological pattern is linear in input length, and the replace returns a fresh string but only walks the input once.

Space is O(L) for the output string — strings are immutable in JS so each `replace` returns a new one (the old `out` reference gets garbage collected after the assignment). Plus O(k * E) for the escaped term regexes, where E is the average term length — basically negligible.

If you wanted me to extend this:
• Single combined regex — `new RegExp('\\b(?:' + terms.map(escape).join('|') + ')\\b', 'gi')` collapses k sweeps into 1. Now O(L) total instead of O(k * L). Win for large term lists.
• Per-term hit count — replace the scalar `count` with a `Map<term, count>` (or `Map<pattern, count>`) and capture the match in the callback: `re.replace(re, (match) => { counts[term]++; return '[REDACTED]'; })`. Useful for audit reports.
• Reversible redaction — store `[REDACTED:abc123]` with a random token, plus an aside-map from token → original text. Decrypt back to original by replacing tokens. Different threat model.
• Differential privacy / hashed redaction — instead of `[REDACTED]`, replace with `[PERSON_001]`, `[PERSON_002]` with a stable hash. Preserves 'this is the same person referenced again' across the doc.
• Other PII patterns — credit cards (Luhn-validated), emails (`/\S+@\S+\.\S+/`), phone numbers (NANP regex), MRNs (org-specific).
• Multi-pass NER — beyond regex, a named-entity-recognition model would catch names that aren't in the term list. The regex+terms approach is the precision-only baseline; NER trades precision for recall.

The template here is: scan + escape user input + replacer-callback for side-effecting counts. Any 'find these patterns and do X' problem maps to the same shape."
sections.why: The single-combined-regex optimization is the right unprompted extension — it shows you see the k-term loop as the bottleneck and know how to collapse it. The reversible / hashed-redaction extension shows threat-model awareness; redaction in legal tech often needs to be reversible by the producing side. The NER mention is the right humility move — regex is a precision tool, not a recall tool; flagging that you know the limit shows the interviewer you wouldn't ship the regex-only redactor as a complete PII solution.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the PII redactor on a real medical note. The state panel shows the running `out` string, the `count` of redactions, the current term being processed, and the regex being built. Watch how the SSN sweep runs first (one scan, multiple hits via `g`), then each term gets its own escaped, word-boundary-anchored, case-insensitive regex.

examples.label: L3 note: 1 SSN + 'Jane' x2 + 'Smith' x1 = 4 redactions

input.text: Patient Jane Doe, SSN 123-45-6789, treated by Dr. Smith. Jane reported pain.

examples.expected: {"text":"Patient [REDACTED] Doe, SSN [REDACTED], treated by Dr. [REDACTED]. [REDACTED] reported pain.","count":4}

examples.label: two SSNs, no terms: g-flag catches both in one sweep

trace: yield { line: 2, label: 'init — count=0, out=original text (' + text.length + ' chars), ' + terms.length + ' sensitive term(s)', state: { text, terms, out, count, phase: 'init' } };

yield { line: 4, label: 'SSN sweep /\\b\\d{3}-\\d{2}-\\d{4}\\b/g — ' + ssnMatches.length + ' hit(s): ' + JSON.stringify(ssnMatches) + ' → count=' + count, state: { text, terms, out, count, phase: 'ssn', ssnHits: ssnMatches } };
yield { line: 7, label: 'term#' + i + " '" + term + "' → escape metachars → '" + escaped + "' (no-op if no special chars)", state: { text, terms, out, count, phase: 'escape', i, term, escaped } };

yield { line: 9, label: 'build regex /\\b' + escaped + '\\b/gi — preview: ' + matches.length + ' match(es) in current out: ' + JSON.stringify(matches), state: { text, terms, out, count, phase: 'build-re', i, term, escaped, matches } };

yield { line: 10, label: 'replace ' + matches.length + " hit(s) with [REDACTED] for term '" + term + "' → count=' + count", state: { text, terms, out, count, phase: 'replaced', i, term, hits: matches.length } };
const result = { text: out, count: count };
yield { line: 12, label: 'return { text, count: ' + count + ' } — total redactions=' + count, state: { text, terms, out, count, returns: JSON.stringify(result) } };

reference.approach: Escaped word-boundary regex sweep per term
notes: `\b` word boundaries make each term match whole words only — 'Smith' won't redact inside 'Smithson', and a short term won't hit substrings of unrelated words.
Each term is run through `.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` to escape regex metacharacters, so a term like 'Dr.' or 'a+b' is matched literally instead of as a pattern.

Flags matter: `g` replaces every occurrence (not just the first) and `i` makes it case-insensitive. Using a replacer function `() => { count++; return '[REDACTED]' }` lets you tally hits while substituting.

Time O((1 + k)·L), Space O(L) — 1 SSN sweep + k term sweeps, each linear in text length L; each replace returns a fresh string but doesn't re-scan inserted text. Collapse k sweeps into one alternation regex to get O(L) if k is large.

questions.q: Why wrap each term in `\b...\b` word boundaries before building the regex?
options: `\b` anchors the regex to the start and end of the string, so the term only matches at the very beginning or end of `text`
So a term matches only whole words — 'Smith' won't redact the 'Smith' inside 'Smithson', and short terms won't hit unrelated substrings
Without `\b`, the `g` flag would only fire once per word and silently skip later occurrences
`\b` is the only way to make the regex emit `[REDACTED]` instead of the raw match into the output
questions.explain: Without `\b`, redacting 'Jan' would also blank out the middle of 'January'. Word boundaries anchor the match to whole tokens, which is what redaction of names/terms requires.

questions.q: Why escape the term with `term.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` before passing it to `new RegExp`?
options: To normalize Unicode combining marks so accented names match their canonical form
To treat regex metacharacters in the term (like the dot in 'Dr.') as literal text instead of pattern syntax
To prevent `new RegExp` from parsing the term as a regex literal `/.../` instead of a string source
To strip the backslashes that JS auto-inserts when reading the term from JSON
questions.explain: A raw '.' in a regex matches any character; '+' or '(' have special meaning too. Escaping turns a user-supplied term into a literal pattern, so 'Dr.' matches only 'Dr.' and not 'Drx'.

questions.q: In `new RegExp('\\b' + escaped + '\\b', 'gi')`, what do the `g` and `i` flags do?
options: `g` = greedy (consume the longest match), `i` = ignore newlines
`g` = replace every occurrence (not just the first), `i` = case-insensitive match
`g` = group the captures, `i` = include surrounding whitespace in the match
`g` = use ASCII mode, `i` = use Unicode (icu) mode
questions.explain: Without `g`, only the first 'Jane' would be redacted. Without `i`, 'jane' in lowercase would slip through. Both flags are needed to catch every occurrence regardless of case.

questions.q: Given the note 'Jane Doe ... Dr. Smith. Jane reported pain.' redacting ['Jane', 'Smith'] plus one SSN, why is the count 4?
options: SSN once + Jane once + Smith once = 3 (the `g` flag dedupes repeated terms across one scan)
SSN once + Jane twice + Smith once = 4
SSN once + each distinct redacted token = 4 ('[REDACTED]' itself, Jane, Smith, the SSN pattern)
Two terms × two passes + SSN sweep + initial baseline = 4
questions.explain: 'Jane' appears twice (start and in 'Jane reported'), 'Smith' once, and the SSN once. The replacer callback increments `count` on each substitution: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4.

exercises.prompt: Redact a US SSN pattern and count the hit using a replacer callback. Fill the blanks.

blanks.hint: increment the tally inside the replacer

exercises.prompt: Build a case-insensitive, whole-word, global regex for a term and replace every match. Fill the flags and the boundary.

L3.prompt: Redact a medical note: replace any SSN (`###-##-####`) and each sensitive term with `[REDACTED]` (case-insensitive, whole-word). Return the redacted text and the redaction count.
L3.expectedOutput:
Patient [REDACTED] Doe, SSN [REDACTED], treated by Dr. [REDACTED]. [REDACTED] reported pain.
Redactions: 4
hints: Match the SSN first with `/\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\b/g` and a replacer callback that increments a counter and returns '[REDACTED]'.
For each term, escape regex metacharacters, then build `new RegExp('\\b' + escaped + '\\b', 'gi')` for whole-word, case-insensitive, global matching.
Return `{ text, count }`; the replacer `() => { count++; return '[REDACTED]'; }` lets you tally while substituting.
